S	solve	the residue theorem	$\oint_{\Gamma_N} Kf\,dz = 2\pi i\left[\sum_{|n| \le N} \operatorname{Res}(Kf, n) + \sum_j \operatorname{Res}(Kf, z_j)\right]$, with $K = \pi\cot\pi z$ or $\pi\csc\pi z$
S	solve	independent cross-check	the quadrature agrees with it to 1.22e-15 — agreement is evidence, not proof — the two share no machinery, which is the point
S	solve	the system	$\sum_i (a_i t + b_i) = \oint_\gamma f(z)\,dz$, solved for $t$
D	solve	=	satisfied		$\oint_\gamma f(z)\,dz = 2\pi i\left(-\frac{115}{72} + \frac{\pi^{2}}{6}\right)$	the orders add at a collision (the kernel's simple pole plus $f$'s order-$2$ one), and the residue comes from the Laurent series of the product rather than the order-$m$ derivative formula, which explodes symbolically from $m = 3$ — the first case being exactly this one · the kernel's residue is exactly $1$ ($\cot$) or exactly $(-1)^n$ ($\csc$) at every integer, so its term is $f(n)$ evaluated exactly over $\mathbb{Q}(i)$; at a pole $z_j$ of $f$ it is $K(z_j)\operatorname{Res}(f, z_j)$, exact as a quotient of basis elements · $\pi\csc(\pi z)$ has a simple pole at every integer with residue $(-1)^n$, and $f$ is regular there, so the residue of the product is the product of the two · the kernel is holomorphic and non-zero at every pole of f, so the residue of the product is the value times the residue; $\csc(\pi z_0)$ is a Möbius function of $e^{2\pi i z_0}$ and therefore an exact quotient of basis elements	
P	solve	true	the kernel's expansion is even — $1/u + \sum_k t_k \pi^{2k} u^{2k-1}$ — so only $c_0$ and the even negative coefficients of $f$ contribute, and the sum is finite at $k \le 1$
P	solve	true	$t_k$ is rational (Bernoulli, from $\sum_j \binom{m+1}{j} B_j = 0$ in exact $\mathbb{Q}$) and the powers of $\pi$ are even, so the value lands in $\mathbb{Q}(i)(\pi)$ — a different ring from the exponential basis G2 solves in, not a harder case of it
P	solve	true	every pole of the cofactor was asked for its winding number and is enclosed once — checked rather than assumed
P	solve	true	at the contour drawn this is $2\pi i$ times the partial sum minus the infinite one; it is the limit $N \to \infty$ that sends it to zero, and that limit is what the vanishing sides establish
P	solve	true	the kernel's residue is a theorem and is asserted; what is computed is $f(n)$, exactly, over $\mathbb{Q}(i)$
P	solve	true	f(0) = —, and no cofactor pole lies on an integer in the band
P	solve	true	the $2\pi i$ of the residue theorem cancels here, because the contour integral tends to zero and the identity is $0 = 2\pi i[\sum f(n) + \sum \operatorname{Res}]$ — so the answer carries the kernel's own $\pi$ and no other
P	solve	true	every pole is simple and Gaussian, which is what makes $e^{2\pi i z_0}$ representable and $K(z_0)\operatorname{Res}(f, z_0)$ the whole residue
D	solve	=	satisfied		$I = −π²/12$	the orders add at a collision (the kernel's simple pole plus $f$'s order-$2$ one), and the residue comes from the Laurent series of the product rather than the order-$m$ derivative formula, which explodes symbolically from $m = 3$ — the first case being exactly this one · the declared collision carries the order arithmetic and the residue, and both are checked against the Laurent route rather than trusted · the kernel is holomorphic and non-zero at every pole of f, so the residue of the product is the value times the residue; $\csc(\pi z_0)$ is a Möbius function of $e^{2\pi i z_0}$ and therefore an exact quotient of basis elements · the unknown sits inside the residue sum, over $\mathbb{Q}(i)(\pi)$: every side of the contour vanishes, so $0 = 2\pi i[wT + \sum \text{merged}]$ and the $2\pi i$ divides out

P	solve	true	the hypothesis that $f$ has no pole at an integer is sufficient for the clean form of the theorem and not necessary for the contour argument, which is why `escalate` is right where `refuse` and `warn` are both wrong
P	solve	true	the $2\pi i$ of the residue theorem cancels here, because the contour integral tends to zero and the identity is $0 = 2\pi i[\sum f(n) + \sum \operatorname{Res}]$ — so the answer carries the kernel's own $\pi$ and no other
